---
title: Authenticate
description: Send a key with data requests, or connect an app with OAuth so the owner approves its access.
---

A program has two ways into Marfa. A script sends a **key**, which begins `marfa_k1_`. An app connects with **OAuth**: the owner approves it once in their browser, and the app receives an access token, which begins `marfa_at_`. Either goes in the same header and reaches only the types and permissions it holds. No program ever needs the owner's password. [Access](/build/access) explains what a credential can hold.

You need your own Marfa instance, with the CLI signed in to it, as the [Quickstart](/quickstart) leaves you.

## Send a key

Make a key for the script, naming each type at the level it needs, as `type=level`:

<Terminal>

```bash
marfa keys create --label "Photo backup" --source photo-backup --type-permission core.file.image=write
```

```text
marfa_k1_…
key 01a1f124-… (Photo backup); the plaintext is shown once, keep it now
  core.file.image  Read and edit
```

</Terminal>

**Keep the key now**: Marfa stores only a hash of it. `--source` names what the script writes as, and [Manage keys](/use/manage-keys) covers expiry, narrowing and rotation.

Send the key as a bearer token on every request; in Swift, give it to `Server(url:key:)`. The CLI takes a key from `MARFA_API_KEY` only with the address of its instance in `MARFA_API_URL`. To check what a key reaches, ask for the key itself:

```bash tab="CLI" tab-group="client"
export MARFA_API_URL=https://marfa.example.com
export MARFA_API_KEY=marfa_k1_…
marfa keys current
```

```http tab="HTTP"
GET /keys/current
Authorization: Bearer marfa_k1_…
```

```ts tab="TypeScript"
import { createClient } from "@withmarfa/client";

const marfa = createClient({
  baseUrl: process.env.MARFA_API_URL ?? "",
  credential: process.env.MARFA_API_KEY ?? "",
});
const { data } = await marfa.GET("/keys/current");
```

The answer names the key's `label`, `source`, `type_permissions` and other permissions, and when it expires and was last used. An app's access token is not a key, so it gets `403 forbidden` here.

## Connect an app with OAuth

An app registers itself, sends the owner to approve it, and exchanges the answer for tokens. The instance is its own authorization server: its discovery document, at `/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server`, names the instance's origin as `issuer` and lists every endpoint under `/oauth/`. **Every client is public**: none holds a secret, and each proves itself with PKCE.

A web page adds a few constraints, which [Connect a web page](/build/connect-a-web-page) covers. In Swift, `Authorization` takes every step for the app, as [the Swift SDK](/reference/swift-sdk#sign-in) shows. An MCP client follows them by itself, starting from the challenge the [MCP server](/reference/marfa-mcp-server) answers.

<Steps>
<Step>

### Register the app

Registration needs no credential:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_name": "Photo frame",
  "application_type": "native",
  "redirect_uris": ["com.example.frame:/callback"],
  "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"],
  "scope": "core.file.image:read offline_access"
}
```

Marfa answers `201` with the `client_id`. A scope is a type and a level, such as `core.file.image:read`, a [permission](/build/access#permissions), or `offline_access` for a refresh token. A registration with no `scope` gets the [default scopes](/catalog/permissions), read and write on your content and its edges, so **name the scopes the app needs**.

The redirect address decides the client's kind:

- A **web** client, the default, uses `https` addresses off the loopback.
- A **native** client may also use `http://127.0.0.1` with any port, or a private-use scheme that is a reverse domain name you control, with a path and no host, as above.

Instead of registering, an app can name itself by a **client ID metadata document**: its `client_id` is the `https` address of a JSON document describing it, which the instance reads when the owner is first sent to approve it. [Register an OAuth client](/reference/api/apps/registerOAuthClient) lists every field.

</Step>
<Step>

### Send the owner to approve

Marfa accepts only PKCE with `S256`. Make a random verifier and keep it:

```bash
verifier=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
challenge=$(printf %s "$verifier" | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=')
```

Open the authorization endpoint in the owner's browser with the challenge and your own `state`:

```http title="Request"
GET /oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=<client_id>&redirect_uri=com.example.frame%3A%2Fcallback&scope=core.file.image%3Aread%20offline_access&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&state=<state>
```

The owner signs in if needed and [approves the app](/connect-your-agent#approve-what-it-may-reach). The page opens on **Full access**, which grants every scope you asked for, and the owner can choose less. A write or a permission needs a sign-in from the last fifteen minutes, so the page may ask the owner to confirm it's them. When the owner already approved these scopes for the app, Marfa skips the page.

Marfa then sends the browser to your redirect address with `code`, `state` and `iss`. Check that **`state` is the one you sent** and that `iss` is the instance's issuer. If the owner denies the app, the redirect carries `error=access_denied` and no code.

</Step>
<Step>

### Exchange the code for tokens

Send the code and verifier to the token endpoint as a form:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=<code>&redirect_uri=com.example.frame%3A%2Fcallback&client_id=<client_id>&code_verifier=<verifier>
```

```json title="Response" status="200"
{
  "access_token": "marfa_at_…",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600,
  "scope": "core.file.image:read",
  "refresh_token": "marfa_rt_…"
}
```

`scope` lists what the owner approved, which **can be less than you asked for**. Send the access token exactly as you would a key. A code works once: sending it again answers `400 invalid_grant` and ends the tokens it gave.

</Step>
<Step>

### Keep the token fresh

Before the access token expires, exchange the refresh token for new ones:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token=marfa_rt_…&client_id=<client_id>
```

The app gets a refresh token only when it asked for `offline_access`. **Each exchange ends the refresh token you sent**, so store the new one first. Sending a used refresh token answers `400 invalid_grant` and ends every token in its chain, because Marfa can't tell which holder is the app. The app then asks the owner again.

</Step>
</Steps>

## Connect an app with the device flow

A command-line tool or a device with no browser uses the OAuth device flow: it shows the owner a short code to approve on another device. `marfa login` signs in this way.

Register as a native client with no redirect address:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "client_name": "Archive tool",
  "application_type": "native",
  "grant_types": ["urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code", "refresh_token"],
  "scope": "core.file:read offline_access"
}
```

Ask for a device code, naming the scopes. A request with no `scope` answers `400 invalid_scope`.

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/device-authorization
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

client_id=<client_id>&scope=core.file%3Aread%20offline_access
```

```json title="Response" status="200"
{
  "device_code": "…",
  "user_code": "8RNZBQH3",
  "verification_uri": "http://localhost:8600/auth/device",
  "verification_uri_complete": "http://localhost:8600/auth/device?user_code=8RNZBQH3",
  "expires_in": 600,
  "interval": 5
}
```

Show the owner the `user_code` and `verification_uri`, or open `verification_uri_complete` for them. Then ask `/oauth/token` for the token, **waiting `interval` seconds between requests**:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/token
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Agrant-type%3Adevice_code&device_code=<device_code>&client_id=<client_id>
```

Until the owner decides, Marfa answers `400 authorization_pending`, or `400 slow_down` when you ask too soon. Approval answers `200` with the same tokens as the code exchange. `400 access_denied` means the owner denied the app, and `400 expired_token` means the code lapsed: start again.

## Revoke access

An app disconnects itself by revoking its refresh token, even one an exchange replaced, which ends its tokens and the owner's approval:

```http title="Request"
POST /oauth/revoke
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

token=marfa_rt_…&token_type_hint=refresh_token&client_id=<client_id>
```

Marfa answers `200` for any token, and changes nothing for an unknown or expired token, another app's, or one whose chain ended.

The owner can narrow or disconnect any app, as [Revoke access](/use/see-and-revoke-access#give-less-access-instead) shows, or with `marfa apps revoke`. A credential that holds `grants.manage` lists apps with `GET /grants`, narrows one with `PATCH /grants/{id}` and disconnects one with `DELETE /grants/{id}`.

## When a request is refused

Branch on **`error.code`, never on the message**:

- `401 unauthorized`: no credential, or one that is unknown, expired or revoked. An app whose access token expired exchanges its refresh token.
- `403 forbidden`: the credential lacks a permission, which `details.required_scope` names.
- `403 type_not_permitted`: the credential can't read or write the type at the level needed, and `details.grant` names the type and level.
- `403` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope"`, from an MCP endpoint: the token lacks the scope a tool call needs, which `scope` names. Send the owner to approve it.
- `404 item_not_found`: the item doesn't exist, or the credential can't read its type. A refusal never tells a credential what it can't see.

The endpoints under `/oauth/` are the exception: they answer errors in OAuth's own shape, `{ "error": "invalid_grant", "error_description": "…" }`, not in the [error envelope](/reference/errors).

The rules behind this page are in the [keys and sign-in](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/keys-and-oauth.md) and [authentication](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/authentication.md) chapters of the contract.
